title: Sweet Tooth, Big Brain: How Fruit Fueled Human Evolution
summary:
Four million years ago, our upright-walking ancestors had brains weighing around 300 grams — about the same as a medium apple. Today, the average human brain weighs 1,500 grams, roughly equal to 1.5 liters of water. Much of that expansion happened before humans mastered fire and cooking. So what fueled it?

A new analysis published in Science points to an overlooked answer: sugar. Researchers combined data from fossils, teeth, metabolism, and biology to calculate the dietary needs of chimpanzees, humans, and three early hominid species. They found that fruit likely provided more than two-thirds of the food energy for our earliest chimp-like ancestors — and sugary carbs remained important as brains grew.

The idea has been building for years. A 2017 study showed that fruit-eating primates had bigger brains than leaf-eating ones. Remembering when different fruits ripen and where to find them places heavy demands on memory and thinking skills. "Your memory is associated with a bigger brain," said Jennie Brand-Miller, a nutrition scientist at the University of Sydney and a lead researcher on the new study.

Fossil primates and later hominids, including Homo erectus, show signs of tooth decay — a clue to a diet rich in soft, sugary foods. "All these things kept adding pieces to this lovely tapestry," Brand-Miller said.

Not everyone agrees that past research ignored sugar. Brian Wood, a biological anthropologist at UCLA, argues that a diverse range of foods — including nuts, honey, and underground plant parts — fueled our evolution, not just one category. But he agrees that meat alone doesn't tell the whole story.

What's clear is that our ancestors needed serious brainpower to find high-energy foods. Hunting, cracking nuts, and extracting bone marrow all require clever foraging. Meat and sugar, Brand-Miller says, are "parallel stories, not one replacing the other."
why_it_matters: The debate matters because it reframes human intelligence as a problem of energy: big brains are only possible if a species can reliably find calorie-rich food. It also complicates simple 'paleo' stories that credit meat alone — and it connects evolution to debates about sugar in modern diets, where the same energy density carries very different health consequences.

background_read: Brain tissue is expensive to run: in modern humans the brain is only about two per cent of body weight but uses roughly a fifth of the body's energy. Any species that grows a bigger brain must either find more high-energy food or spend less energy somewhere else — which is why the question of what our ancestors ate matters so much.

Homo erectus (an early human ancestor that walked upright, made stone tools, and was among the first hominids to move out of Africa) appears in the study's fossil record, and its teeth show signs of decay linked to soft, sugary foods.

The new analysis was published in Science (one of the world's most widely read peer-reviewed journals). It drew on fossils, teeth, metabolism data and biology to estimate what chimpanzees, humans and three early hominid species actually needed to eat.

Anthropologists have long argued about what powered brain growth. Some emphasise meat and bone marrow, because they are calorie-dense. Others, including Harvard biologist Richard Wrangham, argue that cooking was the turning point — cooking softens food and releases more energy, making it easier to feed a costly organ.

Fruit is a patchy resource: different trees ripen in different places at different times, so an animal that lives on it must remember locations and plan routes. That mental demand may be one reason fruit-eating primates, including our ancestors, ended up with bigger brains.

perspectives.description: The study rehabilitates fruit and sugary carbohydrates as serious evolutionary fuel, arguing that our earliest ancestors ate mostly fruit and that carbs remained important as brains expanded. It fits neatly with the memory demands of tracking fruiting trees and with tooth decay in fossil teeth.

Brian Wood of UCLA does not accept that earlier research ignored sugar, and argues that nuts, honey and underground plant parts were equally important. From this view, singling out one food category oversimplifies a diet that was probably broad, seasonal and highly varied.

Whatever the mix, the underlying logic is stable: brain tissue is metabolically costly, so any species with a large brain must solve an energy problem. Meat, fruit, honey, tubers and cooking may each have contributed pieces of that solution rather than competing for the credit.

perspectives.perspective: Forward-looking — from ancestors to modern diets
perspectives.description: The next research step is quantifying how much energy each food type really supplied, using teeth wear, isotopes and living primate behaviour. Meanwhile the finding is easy to misread: sugar in fruit and sugar in processed food are not the same health story, so an evolutionary argument is not a dietary recommendation.
